DIABETES DIETARY GUIDELINES
Clinical Nutrition Reference for Meal Planning & RAG-Based Diet Generation
1. Overview of Diabetes
Type 1 Diabetes: An autoimmune condition in which the pancreatic beta cells are destroyed, resulting in
absolute insulin deficiency. Requires exogenous insulin. Onset is typically in childhood or early adulthood.
Type 2 Diabetes: A metabolic disorder characterized by progressive insulin resistance and relative insulin
deficiency. Strongly associated with obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and genetic predisposition. Accounts for
~90–95% of all diabetes cases worldwide.
Insulin and Glucose: Insulin is a hormone secreted by pancreatic beta cells that facilitates cellular
glucose uptake. In its absence or with reduced sensitivity, blood glucose rises (hyperglycemia), causing
systemic damage over time to kidneys, eyes, nerves, and cardiovascular system.
2. Core Dietary Goals
(cid:127) Stabilize Blood Sugar: Avoid rapid glucose fluctuations by choosing complex carbohydrates and
fiber-rich foods.
(cid:127) Avoid Postprandial Spikes: Target postprandial glucose <140 mg/dL at 2 hours. Limit high-GI foods
and refined sugars.
(cid:127) Improve Insulin Sensitivity: Reduce visceral adiposity through calorie moderation, regular physical
activity, and anti-inflammatory dietary patterns.
(cid:127) Achieve Target HbA1c: Dietary management aims to achieve HbA1c <7% (ADA guideline). Every 1%
reduction decreases microvascular complication risk by ~25%.
3. Carbohydrate Management
Carbohydrates have the greatest direct impact on blood glucose among all macronutrients.
Recommended carbohydrate intake: 45–55% of total daily energy (ADA/ICMR). Emphasis must be
placed on carbohydrate quality, not only quantity.

FIBER RULE: Target 25–35 g/day total dietary fiber (ADA). Soluble fiber (oats, psyllium, legumes) slows
gastric emptying and reduces postprandial hyperglycemia. Insoluble fiber (wheat bran, vegetables)
improves gut motility.
4. Glycemic Index (GI) — CRITICAL REFERENCE
The Glycemic Index (GI) ranks foods (0–100) based on how quickly they raise blood glucose compared to
pure glucose (GI=100). Low GI (<55) foods are preferred for diabetics. Glycemic Load (GL) = (GI × carb
grams per serving) / 100; GL <10 is considered low.

5. Protein Guidelines
Recommended intake: 1.0–1.5 g/kg body weight/day for most T2DM patients (ICMR 2020). Higher
protein intakes (1.2–1.8 g/kg) may be appropriate in obese individuals for weight loss.
Protein causes minimal acute glycemic response. It stimulates insulin secretion modestly and promotes
satiety, reducing overall carbohydrate intake. Protein helps preserve lean muscle mass during
calorie-restricted weight loss programs.

7. Meal Timing & Frequency
(cid:127) Eat 3 main meals + 1–2 small snacks per day; avoid skipping meals.
(cid:127) Space meals 3–4 hours apart to prevent hypoglycemia and excessive hunger.
(cid:127) Avoid prolonged fasting (>6 hours); can trigger reactive hypoglycemia or compensatory overeating.
(cid:127) Eat breakfast within 1–2 hours of waking to stabilize morning glucose.
(cid:127) Keep carbohydrate portions consistent across meals for better glycemic control.
(cid:127) Limit caloric intake after 8 PM; evening meals should be lighter.

10. Clinical Notes & Monitoring
(cid:127) Fiber: Target 25–35 g/day. Introduce gradually to avoid GI discomfort. Psyllium husk, oats, and
legumes are excellent soluble fiber sources.
(cid:127) Hydration: 8–10 glasses of water/day (2–2.5 L). Avoid sugary drinks. Infused water (jeera, cucumber)
is acceptable.
(cid:127) Blood Glucose Monitoring: Fasting target 80–130 mg/dL; 2-hr postprandial <180 mg/dL (ADA).
Self-monitoring guides food choices.
(cid:127) HbA1c Monitoring: Every 3 months until controlled; every 6 months once stable. Target <7%.
(cid:127) Sodium: Limit to <2300 mg/day, especially in hypertensive diabetics.
(cid:127) Alcohol: If consumed, max 1 unit/day with food; monitor for hypoglycemia.
(cid:127) Supplement consideration: Vitamin D, B12, and magnesium deficiencies are common in T2DM
patients and may worsen insulin resistance — assess and supplement if needed.

HYPERTENSION DIET GUIDELINES
Low-Sodium, Heart-Healthy DASH Diet Clinical Reference
1. What is Hypertension?
Hypertension (high blood pressure) is defined as sustained systolic BP ‡130 mmHg and/or diastolic BP
‡80 mmHg (ACC/AHA 2017) or ‡140/90 mmHg (WHO/JNC-7). It affects ~1.28 billion adults worldwide and
is the leading modifiable risk factor for stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and chronic kidney
disease.
Classification Systolic (mmHg) Diastolic (mmHg) Action
Normal <120 <80 Maintain healthy lifestyle
Elevated 120–129 <80 Lifestyle modification
Stage 1 HTN 130–139 80–89 Lifestyle + consider medication
Stage 2 HTN ‡140 ‡90 Medication + intensive lifestyle changes
Hypertensive Crisis >180 >120 Immediate medical attention
2. DASH Diet Overview (CRITICAL)
The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet is the most evidence-based dietary pattern
for BP reduction. Clinical trials show DASH reduces systolic BP by 8–14 mmHg — comparable to a
single antihypertensive medication. The diet is endorsed by AHA, NHLBI, WHO, and ICMR as a first-line
lifestyle intervention.

4. Potassium — Critical Counter to Sodium
Potassium helps kidneys excrete excess sodium and relaxes blood vessel walls. Target: 3500–4700
mg/day from food (NOT supplements unless prescribed; dangerous in CKD/hyperkalemia). Each 1000
mg/day increase in potassium reduces systolic BP by ~1.5–3 mmHg.

8. Lifestyle Advice
Weight Control: Losing 1 kg body weight reduces systolic BP by ~1 mmHg. Target BMI 18.5–24.9.
Physical Activity: 30 min moderate aerobic exercise 5×/week (brisk walking, cycling) reduces BP by
4–9 mmHg.
Alcohol Reduction: Limit to £1 drink/day (women) and £2 drinks/day (men). Excess alcohol raises BP
significantly.
Smoking Cessation: Each cigarette raises BP transiently; chronic smoking hardens arteries. Cessation
is critical.
Stress Management: Chronic stress activates RAAS (renin-angiotensin system), raising BP. Yoga,
meditation, and breathing exercises have evidence.
Sleep: 6–8 hours/night. Sleep apnea and short sleep duration are independent HTN risk factors.

INDIAN DIET GUIDELINES
Culturally Relevant Nutrition Reference for Balanced Meal Planning
1. Overview of Indian Dietary Patterns
The traditional Indian diet is predominantly plant-based, rich in complex carbohydrates, lentils, vegetables,
and dairy, with regional variations based on geography, climate, religion, and cultural practices. However,
modern urban Indian diets increasingly include refined foods, excess salt, sugar, and saturated fat,
contributing to a rising burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) including diabetes, hypertension,
obesity, and cardiovascular disease.

5. The Indian Protein Gap (CRITICAL)
ICMR surveys and NSSO data consistently show that 70–80% of Indian adults consume LESS than the
RDA for protein. Average Indian protein intake = 47g/day vs. recommended 50–60g/day (minimum). For
active individuals, children, pregnant women, and those with metabolic conditions, the gap is even
larger. This is a critical nutritional deficiency driving sarcopenia, poor wound healing, immune
dysfunction, and metabolic disease.

Why is protein low in Indian diets?
(cid:127) Over-reliance on carbohydrates (rice, roti) with inadequate dal/legume portions
(cid:127) Incomplete proteins from plant foods — no single plant food has complete amino acid profile
(cid:127) Low meat, egg, and dairy consumption (vegetarian majority + cost barriers)
(cid:127) Dal often diluted / thin in consistency; portions too small to meet needs
(cid:127) Limited awareness of protein content in foods
Solutions and Protein-Boosting Strategies:
(cid:127) Include at least 1 full cup of cooked dal/legumes per meal (not just a side portion)
(cid:127) Add sprouts to salads, sandwiches, or chaats daily
(cid:127) Combine cereals + legumes (rice + dal, roti + rajma) — improves amino acid completeness
(cid:127) Include paneer, curd, or milk at every meal where possible
(cid:127) Eggs are the highest quality, most affordable protein — include 1–2 daily if dietary practice permits
(cid:127) Soy protein: tofu, edamame, soy milk — underutilized high-quality plant protein
(cid:127) Protein-dense snacks: roasted chana, mixed nuts, Greek yogurt instead of biscuits/namkeen

7. Healthy Indian Cooking Practices
(cid:127) Reduce oil: Use 2–3 tsp/person/meal maximum. Air fry, bake, steam, or grill instead of deep frying.
(cid:127) Ferment: Idli, dosa, dhokla, and fermented chutneys improve bioavailability and gut health.
(cid:127) Use whole grains: Replace 100% maida rotis with whole wheat, multigrain, or millet rotis.
(cid:127) Tadka smartly: Use minimal ghee/oil in tadka; use mustard oil (MUFA-rich) instead of dalda.
(cid:127) Add sprouts to dal: Sprouting increases vitamin C, B vitamins, and mineral bioavailability.
(cid:127) Reduce salt: Use lemon, amchur, tamarind, and spices for flavor instead of extra salt.
(cid:127) Cook tomatoes: Cooking tomatoes increases lycopene bioavailability (heart-protective).
(cid:127) Avoid pressure cooking vegetables excessively: Light steaming or sauteing preserves more
nutrients.

PCOS NUTRITION GUIDELINES
Hormone-Friendly, Insulin-Sensitive Dietary Reference
1. What is PCOS?
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive
age, affecting 6–12% of women globally. It is defined by the Rotterdam Criteria (2 of 3): oligo/anovulation,
clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound.
Insulin Resistance is present in 65–80% of PCOS patients regardless of BMI. Hyperinsulinemia
stimulates ovarian androgen production, worsening hormonal imbalance, acne, hirsutism, and menstrual
irregularity. Addressing insulin resistance through diet is a cornerstone of PCOS management.
2. Dietary Goals
(cid:127) Improve Insulin Sensitivity: Low-GI diet, balanced macros, fiber-rich foods reduce fasting insulin by
20–30%.
(cid:127) Reduce Chronic Inflammation: PCOS is an inflammatory condition. Anti-inflammatory foods
(omega-3, antioxidants) reduce CRP and inflammatory cytokines.
(cid:127) Support Hormonal Balance: Adequate zinc, magnesium, and vitamin D regulate androgen
metabolism and SHBG levels.
(cid:127) Achieve Healthy Weight: Even 5–10% weight loss in overweight PCOS patients restores ovulation in
50–60% of cases.
(cid:127) Gut Microbiome Support: Prebiotic fiber and fermented foods improve estrogen metabolism and
reduce systemic inflammation.
3. Carbohydrate Management
Target carbohydrates: 40–45% of total energy. Emphasize low-GI, high-fiber choices. Avoid refined
carbohydrates as they acutely elevate insulin, worsening androgen excess.

10. Lifestyle Integration
Exercise: 150 min/week moderate aerobic activity (brisk walk, cycling) + 2×/week strength training.
Resistance training improves insulin sensitivity by 25–30% in PCOS.
Sleep: 7–9 hours/night. Poor sleep worsens cortisol, ghrelin (hunger hormone), and insulin resistance.
Sleep apnea is more common in PCOS — screen if indicated.
Stress Management: Chronic stress elevates cortisol and androgens. Yoga, mindfulness, and breathing
exercises (pranayama) have RCT evidence for improving PCOS hormonal markers.
Meal Timing: Front-load calories (larger breakfast, smaller dinner). Late-night eating worsens circadian
insulin resistance.

7. Common Myths & Scientific Clarifications
n MYTH: High protein damages kidneys in healthy people.
n FACT: Extensive meta-analyses (Kalantar-Zadeh 2017; Lowery 2016) confirm that high protein intake
(up to 2.5 g/kg/day) does NOT damage kidneys in healthy individuals. Restriction is ONLY needed in
pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD Stage 3+).
n MYTH: You can only absorb 20–30g protein per meal.
n FACT: There is no 'absorption cap' — the body absorbs all protein, but muscle protein synthesis
(MPS) is maximized at 20–40g per meal. Excess beyond MPS threshold is oxidized for energy or used
for other functions. Spreading protein evenly is OPTIMAL but large amounts are still digested.
n MYTH: Plant protein is inferior and cannot build muscle.
n FACT: Plant proteins can fully support muscle growth when: (a) total intake is adequate, (b)
complementary proteins are combined (rice+dal), and (c) leucine-rich sources like soy, edamame, or a
varied diet are included. Soy protein has DIAAS >0.97.
n MYTH: Protein powders are necessary.
n FACT: Whole food sources are always preferred. Supplements are only needed when whole

oy, edamame, or a
varied diet are included. Soy protein has DIAAS >0.97.
n MYTH: Protein powders are necessary.
n FACT: Whole food sources are always preferred. Supplements are only needed when whole food
intake is consistently inadequate (e.g., athletes >1.8g/kg, post-surgery recovery). Whey, casein, and
pea protein are safe, evidence-based options when whole foods are insufficient.
n MYTH: Excess protein causes obesity.
n FACT: Protein has the highest satiety value and the highest thermic effect (~25–30% of protein
calories burned in digestion). High-protein diets are consistently associated with LOWER total caloric
intake and BETTER weight management outcomes in RCTs.

3. Protein & Metabolism Support
Hypothyroidism slows metabolism and increases muscle protein breakdown. Adequate protein intake
(1.0–1.5 g/kg/day) preserves muscle mass and supports thyroid hormone receptor activity. Protein also
promotes satiety, which counters hypothyroid-associated weight gain.

by the thyroid gland. They are a concern ONLY when: (a) iodine intake is already deficient, or (b)
consumed in very large quantities (especially raw). Cooking reduces goitrogenic activity by 30–60%.

7. Meal Timing
Levothyroxine timing rule (CRITICAL for prescribed patients): Take medication on an empty stomach,
30–60 minutes before breakfast. Avoid coffee, calcium supplements, iron supplements, and high-fiber
meals immediately after medication.
(cid:127) Eat 3 consistent meals per day — metabolic consistency supports thyroid hormone regulation.
(cid:127) Avoid prolonged calorie restriction (<1200 kcal/day) — can further suppress thyroid function.
(cid:127) Spacing meals 4–5 hours apart allows adequate T3 action between meals.
